"Did you check the mercury valve?"

"Like four times, Sam. It's something else."

We had been stuck for weeks. All the math worked out, it was just the damn machine. So many variables had to be adjusted for, so many places where things could go wrong. Discarded coffee cups and takeout boxes littered the floor.

"I'm beginning to think we bit off more than we could chew. Why would we promise them results within a month? It's madness."

"I keep telling you, time doesn't matter, as soon as we succeed then we can- "

"Yes, go back and tell ourselves how to fix the damn thing and then it'll be on time. Where the hell are we anyway?"

Had to admit, if our future selves did succeed, we seemed to be taking our sweet time in contacting ourselves. A loud snap and a chorus of swear words pierced the workshop, emanating from my partner buried in the depths of the machine.

"You OK?"

"Just a bearing. Not important. Although I got a nice cut on my finger."

"I'll get the first aid kit out."

Crossing the workshop, I glance up at the machine which devoured the last few years of our lives. Millions in grant money, down the drain. Years of research, all for a hunk of metal and plastic that couldn't even power up. Muffled expletives broke the silence as I poked thru the kit, looking for some clean gauze. I held up a piece, illuminated in the red glow of the machine.

Wait.

"Tom? You need to come out here, Tom."

"Is the cleaning crew here already? Fuckin building super, I told him-"

"Tom, it's working."

His eyes were bugging out as he climbed from the access panel on the side of the machine. A transparent polymer housing near the front of the machine had filled entirely with what appeared to be a red glowing gas- proof concrete that the fusion tubes had kicked into life.

"This means-"

We abandoned our dignity for a few moments and celebrated. I'm not a very good dancer so I'll spare a description.

"What do you say? Test run?"

"Sam, I don't know. We have phone calls to make, higher-ups to inform. This isn't a convertible that we can take on a joyride."

"Who's gonna know? We have all the time in the world, man."

I glanced at the machine's display. Large red LCD numbers blinked back at us in the current year: 2051.

"We would have to go way back. So theres no chance were found out that we took it for a spin first. "

"That's more like it!" Tom opened up the door to the seating in the machine, dusting off the controls and started pressing buttons.

"I don't know though. What if our numbers are off? We could end up a mile above the earth's surface, or embedded inside a cliff face. We should save this for the official test."

"We've ran the computer simulation a thousand times. It checks before it locks into a date. The only obstacle was that power supply. And I somehow got that to finally stick. Let's do it! I've been waiting my whole life for this moment."

I hesitated fora second more before stepping in the cockpit.

"Fine, buy I pick the year. We're going way back, the Middle Ages." I punched the number 1002 into the LCD display and shut the door.

"Ready to make history?"

A blinding red flash of light, followed by blinding darkness. I open my eyes, and we were surrounded by blue.

Something went wrong. I knew it. Tom was at the controls and shouting something about a building.

Turning around, something is wrong. A lot of the meters and instruments aren't the ones we put in. It looked like an old aircraft cockpit, with altitude meters and a flight stick . We were sitting askew, the top of our machine wedged diagonally inside the other craft.

I looked again at our own instrument panel, at the destination year: 1002. But the angle we were sitting at made me notice something else- one of the buttons controlling that screen was on the left side of the screen. That's not right, the model we used was right-mounted.

Someone had installed the display upside down, I mused. It's funny how the biggest projects are brought low by the simplest mistakes, I thought, as the great grey shape loomed in front of us.
